summary: DNSSEC needs cryptographic algorithms to sign DNS data, and IANA keeps a registry of them but not their recommended implementation status. This applicability statement lists each DNSKEY algorithm's status for DNSSEC software. It was replaced by RFC 8624.

eli5.summary: This is a chart saying which secret-code methods DNS security software should support. A newer chart replaced it.

questions: which dnssec algorithms should be implemented
what is a dnssec applicability statement
subtitle: One table saying which DNSSEC signing algorithms software must, should, may or must not implement.

tldr.problem: The IANA registry lists DNSSEC signature algorithms but not whether implementers should support each one, so they had to read many documents to find out.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement gives every registered algorithm one of four statuses (Must Implement, Must Not Implement, Recommended to Implement, Optional) in a single table, with the rationale.
tldr.outcome: It has been obsoleted by RFC 8624, as the document itself said would happen whenever a status changed, so RFC 8624 holds the current table.

today: RFC 6944 has been obsoleted by RFC 8624, which now holds the algorithm implementation status table. Its design required exactly this kind of replacement whenever a status changed.

sections.title: One Place for Algorithm Status
sections.content:
DNSSEC uses digital signatures over DNS data to provide source authentication and integrity protection. The algorithms behind those signatures (each a cryptographic algorithm plus a one-way hash function) are given codes in an IANA registry.

The original status list was in RFC 4034, and later RFCs added algorithms or changed statuses. Implementers had to read all of them to learn which algorithms were wise to implement. RFC 6944 collects the current status of every registered algorithm in one document, and it updates RFCs 2536, 2539, 3110, 4034, 4398, 5155, 5702 and 5933.
sections.eli5: Before, you had to read a pile of papers to learn which secret codes your software should know. Now there is one page with the answer.

sections.title: The Four Statuses
sections.content:
The document uses RFC 2119 words to define four statuses:

  • Must Implement: the algorithm MUST be implemented to interoperate with other implementations.
  • Must Not Implement: the algorithm MUST NOT be implemented because it has known weaknesses.
  • Recommended to Implement: the algorithm SHOULD be implemented. Interoperability is improved, though there may be reasonable occasions not to, and an implementer must weigh the implications.
  • Optional: the algorithm MAY be implemented, but all implementations MUST be prepared to interoperate with ones that do or do not implement it.
sections.eli5: There are four labels: you must have it, you must not have it, you should have it, or it is up to you. It works like a packing list for a trip.

sections.title: The Status Table and Its Rationale
sections.content:
RSASHA1 is Must Implement, consistent with RFC 4034. RSAMD5 is Must Not Implement because of known weaknesses in MD5. RSASHA256, RSASHA512 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 are Recommended to Implement: many deployments use NSEC3, and major deployments such as the root zone use the SHA-2 RSA algorithms, which are believed likely to replace older algorithms with a perceived weakness.

ECDSAP256SHA256 and ECDSAP384SHA384 are also Recommended to Implement because they may see widespread use, offering similar security with smaller keys than RSA. Everything else is Optional; at the time of writing that meant DSASHA1, DH, DSA-NSEC3-SHA1 and GOST-ECC.

Reserved values and the values for INDIRECT (252), PRIVATE (253) and PRIVATEOID (254) are not in the table because they may relate to more than one algorithm, so they are left to the implementer.
sections.eli5: The old code that is known to be weak is banned. The popular, stronger codes are recommended, and the rest are optional extras.

sections.title: Updating the Table
sections.content:
Algorithms added through the RFC 6014 procedure are automatically Optional. When a new algorithm needs a status other than Optional, or when any status in the table changes, a new document must make RFC 6944 obsolete and replace the table. This document cannot be updated, only obsoleted, so that one document is always the authority.

The IANA considerations note that the document is listed as a reference for the algorithm registry. The security section says no new security considerations are raised, though the earlier description of some algorithms as NOT RECOMMENDED was recast as Must Not Implement.
sections.eli5: When the list needs changing, the whole chart is thrown out and replaced by a new one, so there is only ever one right answer.
